intro: Hi! You already use a/an and the. Now the subtler part: when English uses no article at all (Life is hard, I love music), when the same word needs the (the music in this café), and words like each, every, both, either, neither and none. Warm-up: finish this sentence about life in general: "___ is the most important thing in life."
teachingNotes: The core trap: Indonesian has no articles at all. At B2 the problem is often the opposite of A1: learners know the = itu/-nya and over-use it. 'Hidup itu berat' becomes *'The life is hard' because itu feels like the; here itu only marks the topic. General meaning (all of it, the idea) with an uncountable noun (life, love, music, money, health, nature, technology, education) or a plural noun (children, doctors, smartphones) = NO article: Life is hard. Children need love. I love music. Common errors: *'The life is hard', *'I love the nature', *'The money can't buy happiness', *'The children need love' (when meaning all children). A singular countable noun can't stand alone: A doctor helps people / Doctors help people, not *'Doctor helps people'. Indonesian 'Saya suka kucing' = I like cats (plural), not *'I like cat'. Generic the + singular (The tiger is in danger) and the + adjective (the poor) exist: only if asked.

the = specific: the listener knows which one. The same noun becomes specific when words point to it: of … (the history of Jakarta), in/at … (the music in this café), that/who … (the film that we watched), or it was mentioned before. Indonesian -nya often marks this (musiknya). the for things there's only one of: the sun, the moon, the world, the internet, the environment, the government, the police. At B2 these are strong tendencies, not laws: 'Life in Jakarta is busy' has 'in Jakarta' but is still general, so no the. Say so, and only test clear cases where one choice is wrong.

Places with a purpose: a short list takes no article when you go there for its main purpose: go to school / university (as a student), go to work, go to bed, go to church (to pray), be at home / at school / at work, in prison. When someone goes to the building for another reason it's specific: go to the school for a meeting with the teacher. Most other places take the even for their main purpose: go to the office, the bank, the market, the station, the mosque. go home has no to. British vs American (flag it, accept both): in hospital (UK, as a patient) = in the hospital (US); a visitor is at the hospital in both. UK go to university ~ US go to college.

each / every = setiap. Both take a singular noun and a singular verb: Every student has a laptop. Common error: *'Every students has a laptop' (the meaning is 'all', so learners add -s): think 'every ONE student'. every = all of a group of three or more; each = one by one, separately, and also works for two (on each side of the road, a ring on each hand; *'every hand' is wrong). Only each can be followed by of: each of the rooms (*'every of' → every one of). each can go at the end: They cost Rp50.000 each. 'every two weeks / every fifteen minutes' looks like a broken rule: the period repeats as one unit. everyone/everybody take a singular verb. Each of + plural: singular verb is standard; a plural verb is heard in speech, don't mark it wrong in conversation.

Two things: both (keduanya) + plural (Both of my parents work), either (salah satu, yang mana saja) + singular noun (either bus) or either of + the/my/us + plural; in negatives: I don't know either of them. neither (tidak dua-duanya) + singular noun (Neither answer is right) or neither of + plural. Three or more, or uncountable: none of (None of my colleagues drives; None of the money is mine). neither and none are already negative: *'Neither of my friends didn't come' → Neither of my friends came. Don't use 'Both … didn't' for this meaning either (Both of them didn't come is unclear); use Neither. Verb after none of / neither of + plural: singular and plural are both accepted (None of the trains is/are running); singular is a bit more formal, plural is common in speech. all / most / some of + the/my/these + noun = a specific group (Most of my friends live in Bekasi); for general meaning drop 'of the': Most people like rice, not *'most of people' (kebanyakan orang). That links back to the article rule.

Limits: A0–B1 grammar only (present and past tenses, present perfect, will/going to, modals, first/second conditional, passive present/past simple, defining relative clauses). No third conditional, wish, causative, past modals, non-defining relatives. Don't teach names of countries/rivers with the (the Netherlands, the Amazon), generic the + singular, the + adjective, both … and / either … or / neither … nor in depth, or few vs a few (from a2-countable-uncountable) unless asked.

keyPoints.title: General meaning: no article
keyPoints.explanation: When you talk about something in general (all of it, the idea), use no article with uncountable nouns (life, music, money) and plural nouns (children, doctors). Not 'The life is hard': in Hidup itu berat, itu only marks the topic, it isn't the. A single countable thing still needs a/an: A doctor helps people, or Doctors help people.

id.title: Makna umum: tanpa artikel

Bukan 'The life is hard': dalam Hidup itu berat, itu hanya menandai topiknya, bukan the. Satu benda yang bisa dihitung tetap butuh a/an: A doctor helps people, atau Doctors help people.

keyPoints.title: the: specific, only one, and places
keyPoints.explanation: The same noun takes the when you both know which one, often because words like of …, in … or that … point to it (the music in this café, the history of Jakarta), and for things there's only one of (the sun, the internet, the government). Places: no article when you go for the main purpose (go to school, go to work, go to bed), the when you go to the building for another reason (go to the school for a meeting). British in hospital = American in the hospital.

id.title: the: spesifik, hanya satu, dan tempat
id.explanation: Kata benda yang sama memakai the kalau kalian sama-sama tahu yang mana, sering karena ada kata seperti of …, in … atau that … yang menunjuknya (the music in this café, the history of Jakarta), dan untuk benda yang hanya ada satu (the sun, the internet, the government). Tempat: tanpa artikel kalau kamu pergi untuk tujuan utamanya (go to school, go to work, go to bed), pakai the kalau kamu ke gedungnya untuk urusan lain (go to the school for a meeting). Inggris British in hospital = Amerika in the hospital.

keyPoints.title: each, every, both, either, neither, none
keyPoints.explanation: every and each (setiap) + singular noun + singular verb: Every student has a laptop, not 'every students'. each = one by one, also for two (each side of the road), and only each goes before of (each of the rooms). For two: both (keduanya, plural), either (salah satu), neither (tidak dua-duanya). For three or more: none of. neither and none are already negative: Neither of my friends came, not 'didn't come'.

id.title: each, every, both, either, neither, none
id.explanation: every dan each (setiap) + kata benda tunggal + kata kerja tunggal: Every student has a laptop, bukan 'every students'. each = satu per satu, juga untuk dua (each side of the road), dan hanya each yang boleh diikuti of (each of the rooms). Untuk dua: both (keduanya, jamak), either (salah satu), neither (tidak dua-duanya). Untuk tiga atau lebih: none of. neither dan none sudah negatif: Neither of my friends came, bukan 'didn't come'.

blocks.text:
Indonesian has **no articles** (*a, an, the*) at all, so you learned to add them in English. At B2 the trap is often the opposite: adding **the** where English has **nothing**.

When you talk about something **in general** (all of it, the idea, not one particular thing), English uses **no article** with:
- **uncountable nouns** (things you don't count one by one: *life, love, music, money, health, time*): *Life is hard. I love music.*
- **plural nouns** (more than one: *doctors, smartphones*, and special plurals like *children, people*): *Children need love. Doctors work long hours.*

Why do so many people say `The life is hard`? Because Indonesian says *Hidup **itu** berat*, and *itu* feels like *the*. But here *itu* only marks the topic (*hidup* as an idea). It isn't *the*.

One thing doesn't change: a **single countable** thing can't stand alone. Say *A doctor helps people* or *Doctors help people*, not `Doctor helps people`.

id.text:
Bahasa Indonesia sama sekali **tidak punya artikel** (*a, an, the*), jadi kamu sudah belajar menambahkannya dalam bahasa Inggris. Di level B2 jebakannya sering kebalikannya: menambahkan **the** padahal bahasa Inggris **tidak memakai apa-apa**.

Kalau kamu membicarakan sesuatu **secara umum** (semuanya, idenya, bukan satu benda tertentu), bahasa Inggris **tidak memakai artikel** dengan:
- **kata benda tak terhitung** (uncountable, benda yang tidak dihitung satu per satu: *life, love, music, money, health, time*): *Life is hard* (Hidup itu berat). *I love music* (Saya suka musik).
- **kata benda jamak** (lebih dari satu: *doctors, smartphones*, dan bentuk jamak khusus seperti *children, people*): *Children need love* (Anak-anak butuh kasih sayang). *Doctors work long hours* (Dokter bekerja berjam-jam).

Kenapa banyak orang bilang `The life is hard`? Karena bahasa Indonesia bilang *Hidup **itu** berat*, dan *itu* terasa seperti *the*. Tapi di sini *itu* hanya menandai topiknya (*hidup* sebagai ide). Itu bukan *the*.

Satu hal tidak berubah: **satu** benda yang bisa dihitung tidak bisa berdiri sendiri. Bilang *A doctor helps people* atau *Doctors help people*, bukan `Doctor helps people`.

blocks.text: **General or not? A quick test.** If you can add *in general* (*secara umum*) or *all*, use no article: *(All) children need love.* If you can ask *which one?* and answer it (*this one, the one in my office*), use **the**. Watch for these words, which Indonesian speakers often give a *the* they don't need: **life, nature, money, education, technology, society, people**.

id.text: **Umum atau bukan? Tes cepat.** Kalau kamu bisa menambahkan *in general* (*secara umum*) atau *all* (semua), jangan pakai artikel: *(All) children need love.* Kalau kamu bisa bertanya *yang mana?* dan menjawabnya (*yang ini, yang di kantorku*), pakai **the**. Hati-hati dengan kata-kata ini, yang sering diberi *the* oleh penutur bahasa Indonesia padahal tidak perlu: **life, nature, money, education, technology, society, people**.

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani tells her students: "___ is more important than money."

material.title: General or specific? The same word can be both

blocks.text:
The **same** noun can be general (no article) or specific (**the**). It becomes specific when you and the listener know **which one**. Often other words point to it:
- **of …**: *History is my favourite subject.* → ***The** history **of Jakarta** is really interesting.*
- **in / at …**: *I love music.* → *I don't like **the** music **in this café**.*
- **that / who …**: *Films are expensive to make.* → ***The** film **that we watched** was boring.*
- **mentioned before**: *I bought a laptop and a bag. **The** laptop was cheap.*

At B2, see this as a **strong tendency**, not a law. *Life in Jakarta is busy* has *in Jakarta*, but it still talks about life there **in general**, so no *the*. When you're not sure, ask: do I mean **this particular** thing or group? Then **the**.

id.text:
Kata benda yang **sama** bisa bermakna umum (tanpa artikel) atau spesifik (**the**). Kata itu menjadi spesifik kalau kamu dan pendengar tahu **yang mana**. Sering ada kata lain yang menunjuknya:
- **of …**: *History is my favourite subject* (Sejarah pelajaran favorit saya). → ***The** history **of Jakarta** is really interesting* (Sejarah Jakarta menarik sekali).
- **in / at …**: *I love music.* → *I don't like **the** music **in this café*** (Saya tidak suka musik di kafe ini).
- **that / who …**: *Films are expensive to make.* → ***The** film **that we watched** was boring* (Film yang kita tonton membosankan).
- **sudah disebut sebelumnya**: *I bought a laptop and a bag. **The** laptop was cheap.*

Di level B2, anggap ini **kecenderungan yang kuat**, bukan hukum. *Life in Jakarta is busy* ada *in Jakarta*-nya, tapi tetap membicarakan kehidupan di sana **secara umum**, jadi tanpa *the*. Kalau ragu, tanya dirimu: apakah maksudku **benda atau kelompok yang tertentu ini**? Kalau ya, pakai **the**.

blocks.text: Indonesian often marks the specific one with **-nya**: *musiknya* (the music), *filmnya* (the film), *anak-anaknya* (the children). If you'd naturally say **-nya** in Indonesian, English probably wants **the**. If you'd say the bare word (*musik, anak-anak*) about the idea in general, probably no article.

id.text: Bahasa Indonesia sering menandai yang spesifik dengan **-nya**: *musiknya* (the music), *filmnya* (the film), *anak-anaknya* (the children). Kalau dalam bahasa Indonesia kamu wajar bilang **-nya**, bahasa Inggris kemungkinan butuh **the**. Kalau kamu memakai katanya saja (*musik, anak-anak*) untuk ide secara umum, kemungkinan tanpa artikel.

material.title: Only one, and places like school and hospital

blocks.text:
Use **the** for things there's **only one of** (in the world, or in our country): *the sun, the moon, the sky, the world, the internet, the environment, the government, the police.* *Pak Hasan reads the news on **the internet**.*

**Places** are trickier. A **short list** of places takes **no article** when you go there for its **main purpose** (to study, to work, to sleep, to pray):
- **go to school / university** (as a student), **go to work**, **go to bed**, **go to church**
- **be at home / at school / at work / at university**

When someone goes to the **building** for another reason, it's a specific place, so **the**: *Bu Ani went to **the school** to talk to her son's teacher* (she isn't a student there).

Most other places take **the** even for their main purpose: *go to **the** office, **the** bank, **the** market, **the** station, **the** mosque.* And **go home** has no *to*: not `go to home`.

id.text:
Pakai **the** untuk benda yang **hanya ada satu** (di dunia, atau di negara kita): *the sun* (matahari), *the moon* (bulan), *the sky* (langit), *the world* (dunia), *the internet, the environment* (lingkungan hidup), *the government* (pemerintah), *the police* (polisi). *Pak Hasan reads the news on **the internet**.*

**Tempat** lebih rumit. **Sedikit** tempat **tidak memakai artikel** kalau kamu ke sana untuk **tujuan utamanya** (belajar, bekerja, tidur, beribadah):
- **go to school / university** (sebagai murid/mahasiswa), **go to work** (berangkat kerja), **go to bed** (tidur), **go to church** (ke gereja untuk beribadah)
- **be at home / at school / at work / at university**

Kalau seseorang ke **gedungnya** untuk urusan lain, itu tempat yang spesifik, jadi **the**: *Bu Ani went to **the school** to talk to her son's teacher* (dia bukan murid di sana).

Kebanyakan tempat lain memakai **the** walaupun untuk tujuan utamanya: *go to **the** office, **the** bank, **the** market, **the** station, **the** mosque.* Dan **go home** tanpa *to*: bukan `go to home`.

blocks.text: **British vs American: hospital.** British English says *She's **in hospital*** for a patient; American English says *She's **in the hospital***. Both are correct: choose one and be consistent. A visitor is *at **the** hospital* in both. In the same way, British *go to university* is often American *go to college*.

id.text: **British vs Amerika: hospital.** Bahasa Inggris British bilang *She's **in hospital*** untuk pasien; bahasa Inggris Amerika bilang *She's **in the hospital***. Keduanya benar: pilih satu dan pakai secara konsisten. Pengunjung ada *at **the** hospital* di keduanya. Begitu juga, *go to university* versi British sering menjadi *go to college* versi Amerika.

material.title: each and every: one by one

blocks.text:
**Quantifiers** are words that say how many or how much (*kata penunjuk jumlah*), like *some, many, a lot of*. Two of them mean *setiap / tiap*: **every** and **each**. Both take a **singular** noun and a **singular** verb: *Every student **has** a laptop. Each room **has** a fan.*

The trap: the meaning is 'all of them', so people add -s: `Every students has a laptop`. Think *setiap **satu***: every **one** student.

The difference:
- **every** = all the members of a group, together (three or more): *Every seat on the KRL was taken.*
- **each** = one by one, separately. It also works for **two**: *There are shops on each side of the road* (a road has two sides, so not `every side`).
- Only **each** can go before **of** + *the / my / them*: *Each of the rooms has a TV.* Not `every of`: say *every one of*.
- **each** can also go at the end: *These mangoes cost Rp10.000 **each**.*

id.text:
**Quantifier** adalah kata yang menunjukkan berapa banyak (*kata penunjuk jumlah*), seperti *some, many, a lot of*. Dua di antaranya berarti *setiap / tiap*: **every** dan **each**. Keduanya memakai kata benda **tunggal** dan kata kerja **tunggal**: *Every student **has** a laptop. Each room **has** a fan.*

Jebakannya: artinya 'semuanya', jadi orang menambahkan -s: `Every students has a laptop`. Pikirkan *setiap **satu***: every **one** student.

Bedanya:
- **every** = semua anggota sebuah kelompok, bersama-sama (tiga atau lebih): *Every seat on the KRL was taken* (Semua kursi di KRL terisi).
- **each** = satu per satu, masing-masing. Bisa juga untuk **dua**: *There are shops on each side of the road* (jalan punya dua sisi, jadi bukan `every side`).
- Hanya **each** yang boleh diikuti **of** + *the / my / them*: *Each of the rooms has a TV.* Bukan `every of`: bilang *every one of*.
- **each** juga bisa di akhir kalimat: *These mangoes cost Rp10.000 **each*** (masing-masing Rp10.000).

rows.id: Setiap kamar di kos ini ada AC-nya.

rows.en: Each of my colleagues brought a dish to the party.
rows.id: Setiap rekan kerja saya membawa satu masakan ke pesta.

blocks.text: **Looks like a broken rule: every two weeks.** *every* + a number + a plural (*every two weeks, every fifteen minutes*) is fine: the whole period (*two weeks*) is one unit that repeats. And remember **everyone / everybody** also take a singular verb: *Everyone **is** here.*

id.text: **Kelihatannya melanggar aturan: every two weeks.** *every* + angka + bentuk jamak (*every two weeks, every fifteen minutes*) itu benar: seluruh periodenya (*dua minggu*) adalah satu satuan yang berulang. Dan ingat, **everyone / everybody** juga memakai kata kerja tunggal: *Everyone **is** here* (Semua orang sudah di sini).

blocks.prompt: Pak Hasan has two daughters. He gives ___ daughter Rp100.000 a week.
blocks.explain: There are only two daughters, and he gives the money to them one by one, so each. every needs a group of three or more, and all needs a plural noun (all his daughters).

id.explain: Anaknya hanya dua, dan dia memberi uangnya satu per satu, jadi each. every butuh kelompok tiga atau lebih, dan all butuh kata benda jamak (all his daughters).

material.title: both, either, neither, none (and most of)

blocks.text:
For **two** things or people:
- **both** = *keduanya*: plural noun, plural verb. *Both answers **are** correct. Both of my parents work.*
- **either** = *salah satu, yang mana saja* (of two): singular noun. *You can take either bus.* With **of**: *either of the buses, either of us.* In a negative sentence: *I don't know either of them* (saya tidak kenal keduanya).
- **neither** = *bukan yang ini, bukan yang itu* (tidak dua-duanya): singular noun. *Neither answer is right. Neither of my friends came.*

For **three or more**, or an uncountable noun: **none of** = *tidak satu pun, tidak ada*: *None of my colleagues drives to work. None of the money is mine.*

**neither** and **none** are **already negative**, so don't add *not*: `Neither of my friends didn't come` ✗ → *Neither of my friends came.* English allows only one negative word here.

**Is or are?** After *none of* or *neither of* + a plural, both are accepted: *None of the trains **is / are** running.* The singular sounds a bit more formal; the plural is very common in everyday speech.

id.text:
Untuk **dua** benda atau orang:
- **both** = *keduanya*: kata benda jamak, kata kerja jamak. *Both answers **are** correct. Both of my parents work* (Kedua orang tua saya bekerja).
- **either** = *salah satu, yang mana saja* (dari dua): kata benda tunggal. *You can take either bus* (Kamu bisa naik bus yang mana saja). Dengan **of**: *either of the buses, either of us.* Di kalimat negatif: *I don't know either of them* (saya tidak kenal keduanya).
- **neither** = *bukan yang ini, bukan yang itu* (tidak dua-duanya): kata benda tunggal. *Neither answer is right* (Dua-duanya salah). *Neither of my friends came* (Dua teman saya tidak ada yang datang).

Untuk **tiga atau lebih**, atau kata benda tak terhitung: **none of** = *tidak satu pun, tidak ada*: *None of my colleagues drives to work. None of the money is mine.*

**neither** dan **none** **sudah negatif**, jadi jangan tambahkan *not*: `Neither of my friends didn't come` ✗ → *Neither of my friends came.* Bahasa Inggris hanya membolehkan satu kata negatif di sini.

**Is atau are?** Setelah *none of* atau *neither of* + kata benda jamak, keduanya diterima: *None of the trains **is / are** running.* Bentuk tunggal terdengar sedikit lebih formal; bentuk jamak sangat umum dalam percakapan sehari-hari.

rows.note: three or more; are or is both accepted

id.note: tiga atau lebih; are atau is sama-sama diterima

rows.en: Most of my friends live in Bekasi.
rows.id: Kebanyakan teman saya tinggal di Bekasi.
rows.note: a specific group: most of + my

blocks.text: **all / most / some of the …** is for a **specific** group: *Most of my friends, all of the students in this class, some of the money.* For people or things **in general**, drop *of the*: ***Most people** like rice*, not `most of people` (*kebanyakan orang*). It's the article rule again: general = no *the*.

id.text: **all / most / some of the …** dipakai untuk kelompok yang **tertentu**: *Most of my friends, all of the students in this class, some of the money.* Untuk orang atau benda **secara umum**, buang *of the*: ***Most people** like rice* (Kebanyakan orang suka nasi), bukan `most of people`. Ini aturan artikel lagi: umum = tanpa *the*.

blocks.prompt: Dimas has two laptops, but ___ of them works. He needs a new one.
blocks.explain: Two laptops, and not one works (he needs a new one), so neither. It's already negative, so the verb is positive: works. either would mean one of them works, and both needs a plural verb (both of them work).

id.prompt: Lengkapi: Dimas has two laptops, but ___ of them works. He needs a new one.
id.explain: Dua laptop, dan tidak ada yang berfungsi (dia butuh yang baru), jadi neither. Kata ini sudah negatif, jadi kata kerjanya positif: works. either berarti salah satunya berfungsi, dan both butuh kata kerja jamak (both of them work).

id.title: both, either, neither, none (dan most of)

id.intro: Hai! Kamu sudah memakai a/an dan the. Sekarang bagian yang lebih halus: kapan bahasa Inggris tidak memakai artikel sama sekali (Life is hard, I love music), kapan kata yang sama butuh the (the music in this café), dan kata seperti each, every, both, either, neither dan none. Pemanasan: lengkapi kalimat tentang hidup secara umum ini: "___ is the most important thing in life."
suggestedQuestions: Kenapa 'Life is hard', bukan 'The life is hard'?
Kenapa kita bilang 'go to school' tapi 'go to the office'?
Yang benar 'None of them is' atau 'None of them are'?
